<thinking>
Looking at the SHAP dependence plot for the feature "yr":

- X-axis: yr values (0 = 2011, 1 = 2012)
- Y-axis: SHAP value (contribution to log demand)

From the plot:
- When yr = 0 (2011): SHAP values are clustered around -0.15 to -0.5, mostly negative (around -0.25 to -0.35 on average)
- When yr = 1 (2012): SHAP values are clustered around +0.1 to +0.28, mostly positive

This is a clear step change - going from 2011 to 2012 shifts the contribution from negative to positive. The effect is a binary/step change since yr is essentially a binary feature (0 or 1).

The importance rank is 2 out of 9, making it the second most important feature.

Direction: Higher yr value (2012 vs 2011) raises predicted demand.
Shape: Step change (binary feature).
Peak: yr = 1 (2012) has the highest contribution.
</thinking>

[EFFECT] The year has a clear step-change effect on predicted bike demand: hours from 2011 consistently lower the model's demand forecast (contributions roughly −0.15 to −0.50 in log space), while hours from 2012 consistently raise it (contributions roughly +0.05 to +0.30). There is no gradual shift — the model treats the two years as fundamentally different demand environments, with 2012 being the higher-demand year.

[IMPORTANCE] This is the second most important feature out of nine, meaning the year a given hour belongs to is one of the strongest drivers of predicted rental volume in the entire model — only one other feature has a greater influence.

[RECOMMENDATION] The strong year-over-year growth captured by the model suggests that overall system demand can increase substantially from one year to the next; planners should build in capacity reviews and fleet scaling annually rather than assuming demand stays flat over time.
